## Warm-up

0.  Describe what EACH of the str\_ functions below does. Then, create a
    new variable "month" which is the two digit month from
    album_release_date

```{r}
spot_new <- spot_smaller |>
  select(title, album_release_date) |>
  mutate(title_length = str_length(title), 
         #Number of characters in title
         year = str_sub(album_release_date, 1, 4), 
         #Pulls of first to fourth character to get year
         title_lower = str_to_lower(title), 
         #makes titles all lowercase
         album_release_date2 = str_replace_all(album_release_date, "-", "/"),
         #Change dates from having dash to slash
         month = str_sub(album_release_date, 6, 7))
spot_new
         
max_length <- max(spot_new$title_length)

str_c("The longest title is", max_length, "characters long.", sep = " ")
#Tells R to combine the 3 strings, seperated by a space, into 1 string 

str_glue("The longest title is {max_length} characters long.")
#Puts max_length into the larger string
```


1.  Identify the input type and output type for each of these examples:

```{r}
str_view(spot_smaller$subgenre, "pop")
typeof(str_view(spot_smaller$subgenre, "pop"))
class(str_view(spot_smaller$subgenre, "pop"))
#Input string, output character

str_view(spot_smaller$subgenre, "pop", match = NA)
typeof(str_view(spot_smaller$subgenre, "pop", match = NA))
#Input: String; Output: character

str_view(spot_smaller$subgenre, "pop", html = TRUE)
typeof(str_view(spot_smaller$subgenre, "pop", html = TRUE))
#Input: string; Output: list

str_subset(spot_smaller$subgenre, "pop")
typeof(str_subset(spot_smaller$subgenre, "pop"))
#Input: string; Output: character 

str_detect(spot_smaller$subgenre, "pop")
typeof(str_detect(spot_smaller$subgenre, "pop"))
#Input: string; Output: logical
```


1: Input string, output character

2: Input: String; Output: character

3: Input: string; Output: list

4: Input: string; Output: character 

5: Input: string; Output: logical

3.  Find the mean song title length for songs with "pop" in the subgenre
    and songs without "pop" in the subgenre.

```{r}
spot_smaller |>
  mutate(title_length = str_length(title), 
    sub_pop = str_detect(subgenre, "pop"), 
    sub_pop = ifelse(sub_pop == TRUE, "Genre with Pop", "Genre without Pop")) |>
  group_by(sub_pop) |>
  summarize(mean_title_length = mean(title_length))
  
```

4.  In the bigspotify dataset, find the proportion of songs which
    contain "love" in the title (track_name) by playlist_genre.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

bigspotify <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/master/data/2020/2020-01-21/spotify_songs.csv')

bigspotify |>
  select(playlist_genre, track_name) |>
  mutate(track_name = str_to_lower(track_name), 
         first_five_letters = str_sub(track_name, 1, 5)) |>
  mutate(has_love = str_detect(track_name, " love "), 
         start_love = str_detect(first_five_letters, "love "),
         love = ifelse(has_love == TRUE, TRUE, 
                       ifelse(start_love == TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)))|>
  filter(!is.na(love)) |>
  group_by(playlist_genre) |>
  summarize(mean = mean(love))
```


5.  Given the corpus of common words in stringr::words, create regular
    expressions that find all words that:

-   Start with “y”.

```{r}
str_subset(words, "^y")
```

-   End with “x”

```{r}
str_subset(words, "x$")
```

-   Are exactly three letters long.

```{r}
str_subset(words, "^...$")
```


-   Have seven letters or more.

```{r}
str_subset(words, "^.......")
```

-   Start with a vowel.

```{r}
str_subset(words, "^[aeiou]")
```


-   End with ed, but not with eed.

```{r}
str_subset(words, "[^e]ed$")
```


-   Words where q is not followed by u. (are there any in `words`?)

```{r}
str_subset(words, "q[^u]")
```
There are no cases of a q followed by not a u.

9.  Create some strings that satisfy these regular expressions and
    explain.

-   `"^.*$"`
```{r}
str_detect("abc", "^.*$")
```

String: "abc". The regular expression needs the string to start, have any number of any characters (including 0), and then end. Any string will match these requirements. 

-   `"\\{.+\\}"`

```{r}
str_detect("{aaaaaaaaa}", "\\{.+\\}")
```

String: "{aaaaaaaaa}". The regular expression needs there to be at least one character surrounded by curly brackets.



-   Have two or more vowel-consonant pairs in a row.

```{r}

```

13. Which decades are popular for playlist_names? Using the bigspotify
    dataset, try doing each of these steps one at a time!

-   filter the bigspotify dataset to only include playlists that include
    something like "80's" or "00's" in their title.
-   create a new column that extracts the decade
-   use count to find how many playlists include each decade
-   what if you include both "80's" and "80s"?
-   how can you count "80's" and "80s" together in your final tibble?

```{r}
bigspotify |>
  distinct(playlist_name) |>
  filter(str_detect(playlist_name, "\\d0'?s")) |>
  mutate(decade = str_extract(playlist_name, "\\d0'?s"), 
         decade = str_replace(decade, "'", "")) |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  summarize(count = n())
```


14. Describe to your groupmates what these expressions will match, and
    provide a word or expression as an example:

-   `"(.)\\1\\1"`
This expression will match any three of the same character in a row. 

```{r}
str_detect("aaa", "(.)\\1\\1")
```

-   `"(.)(.)(.).*\\3\\2\\1"`
This expression will match when a three letter sequence appears and then after any number of characters comes up again but in reverse. 

```{r}
str_detect("racecar", "(.)(.)(.).*\\3\\2\\1")
```


Which words in `stringr::words` match each expression?

```{r}
as_tibble(words) |>
  filter(str_detect(words, "(.)\\1\\1"))

as_tibble(words) |>
  filter(str_detect(words, "(.)(.)(.).*\\3\\2\\1"))
```

No words in words matches the first condition, but paragraph meets the second.

17. BEFORE RUNNING IT, explain to your partner(s) what the following R
    chunk will do:
    
BEFORE: R will call sentences, the replace every occurrence of the following pattern: one or more not space characters followed by a space followed by a second set of one or more not space characters followed by a space followed a third set of one or more not space characters. R will then replace eatch map of the pattern with the first set of one or more not space characters followed by a space followed by the original thrid set of one or more not space characters followed by a space followed by the original second set of one more not space characters. More practically, this will take a grouping of three words/abbreviations that are separated by a space, and then reorder them so the first word comes first, then the third word, then the second word.  

```{r}
sentences |> 
  str_replace("([^ ]+) ([^ ]+) ([^ ]+)", "\\1 \\3 \\2") |> 
  head(5)
```

19. What words in `stringr::words` have the highest number of vowels? What words have the highest proportion of vowels? (Hint: what is the denominator?)  Figure this out using the tidyverse and piping, starting with `as_tibble(words) |>`.

```{r}
as_tibble(words) |>
  mutate(og_length = str_length(value), 
         value_vowls = str_remove_all(value, "[^aeiou]"), 
         new_length = str_length(value_vowls),
         prop_vowls = new_length / og_length) |>
  filter(new_length == max(new_length) | prop_vowls == max(prop_vowls))

```

The maximum number of vowels in a word is 5 and is in appropriate, associate, available, colleague, encourage, experience, individual, and television. The highest proportion of vowels is 1, and is in a. 


20. *Carefully* explain what the code below does, both line by line and in general terms.

```{r}
temp <- str_replace_all(words, "^([A-Za-z])(.*)([a-z])$", "\\3\\2\\1")
as_tibble(words) |>
  semi_join(as_tibble(temp)) |>
  print(n = Inf)
```

Line by Line: 
1: R takes the collection of words in "words", notices any string that begins with an upper or lower case letter, followed by any number (including 0) characters, and then ends with a lowercase letter, and then R replaces the matches with a new order of the same characters, the new string starts with the last lowercase letter, is followed by the any number of characters in the middle, and then ends with the starting uppercase letter. Then R stores this string as temp. 
2: R takes "words" and turns it into a tibble
3: R creates a new tibble that returns all rows in words tibble that match with a row in the tibble version of temp
4: R prints the whole tibble. 

In General:
We create temp that has all the words in "words" but with their first and last letter switched. This is then joined with the words tibble, so we are left with all the words in words that have the same first letter as last letter. 

```{r}

library(httr)
library(rvest)
library(polite)
coco <- "https://www.metacritic.com/movie/coco-2017/" |>
  bow() |> 
  scrape()

top_reviews <- 
  "https://www.metacritic.com/movie/coco-2017/critic-reviews/" |> 
  bow() |> 
  scrape()
top_reviews <- html_nodes(top_reviews, ".leading-normal")
top_reviews <- html_text(top_reviews)

user_reviews <- 
  "https://www.metacritic.com/movie/coco-2017/user-reviews" |> 
  bow() |> 
  scrape()
user_reviews <- html_nodes(user_reviews, ".leading-normal")
user_reviews <- html_text(user_reviews)
```


21. `top_reviews` is a character vector containing the 10 most recent critic reviews for Coco, while `user_reviews` is a character vector with the 50 most recent user reviews (although many are truncated).

a) Print out the user reviews where the reviewer mentions "emotion" or "cry".  Think about various forms ("cried", "emotional", etc.)  You may want to turn reviews to all lower case before searching for matches.

```{r}

  mutate(value = str_to_lower(value)) |>
  filter(str_detect(value, "cry|cried|crying|emotion|emotional|emotions"))
```

There are 11 reviews that mention variations on emotion and crying. There seem to be 2 reviews in Spanish and one in maybe Russian, and I did not search these reviews for similar words in these languages.

```{r}
str_replace(top_reviews, "Pixar", "Pixar Animation Studio")
```


c) Find out how many times each user uses "I" in their review.  Remember that it could be used as upper or lower case, at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence, etc.

```{r}
#Trying to account for options I, I'm, I've, I'll, ect. 
#I_ALL column represents the total number of "I"s in each review

as_tibble(user_reviews) |>
  mutate(I_begining = str_detect(value, "^([Ii] )|^([Ii]')"), 
         I_end = str_detect(value, " [Ii]$|( [Ii]'.)$|([Ii]'..)$"),
         I_beg_length = ifelse(I_begining == TRUE, 1, 0),
         I_end_length = ifelse(I_end == TRUE, 1, 0), 
         I_middle_length = str_count(value, " [Ii] | [Ii]'"), 
         I_ALL = I_beg_length + I_middle_length + I_end_length)|>
  select(value, I_ALL) |>
  print(n=50)

#Still not accounting for reviews in other languages.
```


d) Do critics or users have more complex reviews, as measured by average number of commas used?  Be sure your code weeds out commas used in numbers, such as "12,345".

```{r}
#Average number of commas in user reviews: 
as_tibble(user_reviews) |>
  mutate(commas = str_count(value, "[^\\d],[^\\d]")) |>
  summarize(mean_user_commas = mean(commas))

#Average number of commas in critic reviews: 
as_tibble(top_reviews) |>
  mutate(commas = str_count(value, "[^\\d],[^\\d]")) |>
  summarize(mean_critic_commas = mean(commas))
```

Going by number of commas, users have more complex reviews with a higher number of commas used.
